planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grand Nain is a standard Cavendish-type banana with much less cold tolerance than Orinoco or Musa basjoo, so treat it as a container plant or overwinter with heavy protection in zone 9.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Grand Nain is the commercial Cavendish-type banana grown worldwide for fresh export and the variety most home gardeners already know from the grocery store. Fruit is medium-sized, thin-skinned, and sweet with the familiar mild banana flavor, produced on a comparatively shorter, sturdier pseudostem than many tropical banana cultivars, which helps it stand up better to wind. Unlike Gulf South stalwarts such as Orinoco, Grand Nain has little cold tolerance and the rhizome can be killed outright by a hard freeze rather than simply resprouting, so zone 9 gardeners should grow it in a large container that can be moved to shelter for winter, or commit to heavy mulching and wrapping in a protected microclimate. Full sun, high heat, consistent moisture, and rich soil with regular feeding all speed the roughly 12-15 months it takes from planting to a full bunch of fruit.

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Thousand Fingers is grown mainly as a novelty and ornamental for its enormous, densely packed bunch of tiny fingers rather than for the small fruit itself.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Thousand Fingers is a novelty banana famous for producing an enormous bunch made up of hundreds to over a thousand tiny, finger-length fruits packed densely around a long, extended stalk, making it more of a conversation piece and ornamental curiosity than a practical fruiting banana. The individual fingers are small, mildly sweet, and mostly seedless in cultivated forms, edible but not a substantial harvest compared to standard dessert bananas. The plant itself is tall and vigorous with typical bold tropical banana foliage, and the extraordinarily long bloom stalk with its cascade of tiny fruit is the main reason gardeners grow it. Like most tropical Musa acuminata types it has little cold tolerance in zone 9, so plan on container culture or heavy winter protection, and give it full sun, high heat, and consistent moisture and feeding through the long growing season it needs to bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Praying Hands is grown for its unusual fused fruit as much as for eating, and performs best treated as a container plant in zone 9 given its limited cold tolerance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Praying Hands is a novelty banana whose individual fingers fuse together in pairs along most of their length, opening only at the tips, so each fused pair resembles a pair of hands pressed together in prayer. The fruit itself is sweet and fully edible, similar in flavor to a standard dessert banana, but it is grown chiefly as a talking-point specimen for its unusual form rather than for volume production. Plants have the typical bold, tropical Musa acuminata habit and need the same rich, moist soil, full sun, and heavy feeding as other dessert bananas to fruit well. Cold tolerance is limited, so in zone 9 grow it in a large container that can be sheltered over winter, or provide substantial protection to the rhizome if planting in the ground, since a hard freeze can kill the below-ground growing point outright rather than allowing simple resprouting.

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Ae Ae is grown chiefly for its dramatic white-and-green variegated foliage and fruit and needs protection from cold and strong wind, which can shred the tender leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade after the last frost, in a spot sheltered from strong wind; Ae Ae is a historic Hawaiian banana cultivar prized above all for its striking variegation, with broad white-and-green striped leaves and fruit that also shows white-and-green striping before ripening to a more solid yellow. It is grown as much as an ornamental tropical foliage specimen as for its sweet, edible fruit, and the variegated leaves are notably more prone to wind tatter and sunscald than solid-green banana cultivars, so a protected courtyard or the shelter of taller plantings improves its appearance. Because variegated plants generally grow more slowly than their all-green counterparts, give Ae Ae rich soil, consistent moisture, and regular feeding to keep it vigorous. Cold tolerance is limited like most ornamental Musa cultivars, so plan on container culture or serious winter protection in zone 9.

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the compact 6-8 foot height of Dwarf Red makes it easier to protect or overwinter in a container than taller banana cultivars in zone 9.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Dwarf Red is a compact banana cultivar that stays a manageable 6-8 feet tall, considerably shorter than most fruiting bananas, with maroon-red pseudostems and leaf undersides that add ornamental color even before fruiting. The fruit itself has reddish-purple skin and a rich, dense, sweet flesh, ripening on a smaller bunch than standard dessert bananas but with good flavor for fresh eating. The compact size is the main practical advantage for zone 9 growers, since a Dwarf Red planted in a large container is much easier to move to shelter or wrap for winter protection than an 12-15 foot tropical banana. Give it rich soil, consistent moisture, and regular feeding through the growing season, and protect the rhizome from hard freezes, since like most Musa acuminata types it has limited cold tolerance compared to Orinoco or Musa basjoo.
